results.title: Formation generated by a finite group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite group $G$, the formation generated by $G$ is the class of finite groups $H$ such that $H$ belongs to every formation that contains $G$; that is, it is the intersection of all formations containing $G$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 16.31 for finite groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement (V. A. Vedernikov) that for every finite group $G$ only finitely many formations of finite groups are contained in the formation generated by $G$. Here formations may be empty, and a formation $\mathfrak{F}$ is contained in the formation generated by $G$ when every finite group in $\mathfrak{F}$ belongs to the formation generated by $G$.

results.title: The formation generated by a finite group can have infinitely many subformations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a finite group $G$ such that infinitely many formations are contained in the formation generated by $G$. That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 16.31 is negative, even for finite $G$.

results.title: Norm of an automorphism of a free group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F_n$ be the free group on the basis $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, and for $w \in F_n$ let $|w|$ be the length of the reduced word representing $w$. The norm of an automorphism $\alpha$ of $F_n$ is $\|\alpha\| = \max(|\alpha(x_0)|, \dots, |\alpha(x_{n-1})|)$, taken to be $0$ when $n = 0$.

results.title: Fixed subgroup of a free group automorphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an automorphism $\alpha$ of the free group $F_n$ on $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, the fixed subgroup of $\alpha$ is the subgroup $\mathrm{Fix}(\alpha) = \{x \in F_n \mid \alpha(x) = x\}$ of $F_n$.

results.title: Fixed subgroups with a short free basis
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an automorphism of the free group $F_n$ on $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, let $|w|$ be the length of the reduced word representing $w \in F_n$, and let $L$ be a natural number. The fixed subgroup $\mathrm{Fix}(\alpha)$ has a short free basis with bound $L$ when, for some $k \ge 0$, it has a free basis $y_1, \dots, y_k$ with $|y_i| \le L$ for every $i$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 14.23, rank-dependent form
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every $n$ there is a computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every automorphism $\alpha$ of the free group $F_n$ on $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, the fixed subgroup $\mathrm{Fix}(\alpha)$ has a finite free basis all of whose elements have reduced word length at most $f(\|\alpha\|)$, where $\|\alpha\|$ is the maximum of the reduced word lengths of $\alpha(x_0), \dots, \alpha(x_{n-1})$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 14.23, rank-uniform form
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Kourovka Problem 14.23 holds for each rank
results.caption: Theorem

results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Encoded words in a free group of finite rank

results.title: Smallest denominator in an interval
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For real numbers $x$ and $\delta$, the smallest denominator $q_{\min}(x, \delta)$ is the least positive integer $q$ for which there is an integer $p$ with $|x - p/q| < \delta/2$, that is, with $p/q$ in the open interval $(x - \delta/2, x + \delta/2)$. If there is no such $q$, which happens only when $\delta \le 0$, then $q_{\min}(x, \delta) = 0$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $\delta$ be real numbers, let $q$ be a positive integer and let $p$ be an integer. If $|x - p/q| < \delta/2$, then the smallest denominator satisfies $q_{\min}(x, \delta) \le q$.

results.title: Every real number has arbitrarily close rationals
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: The smallest denominator is positive and attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real number $x$ and every real $\delta > 0$, the smallest denominator $q = q_{\min}(x, \delta)$ is positive and there is an integer $p$ with $|x - p/q| < \delta/2$.

results.title: Minimality of the smallest denominator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $\delta$ be real numbers and let $q$ be a positive integer with $q < q_{\min}(x, \delta)$, where $q_{\min}(x, \delta)$ is the smallest denominator. Then there is no integer $p$ with $|x - p/q| < \delta/2$.

results.title: Upper bounds on the smallest denominator

results.title: Wide intervals have smallest denominator one

results.title: Instances of LONGEST CYCLE
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of LONGEST CYCLE is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges), and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

results.title: Graph of a LONGEST CYCLE instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE, its graph is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$. Loops are dropped, and pairs with an endpoint at least $n$ contribute no edge.

results.title: Well-formed LONGEST CYCLE instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.

results.title: Feasible LONGEST CYCLE instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE is feasible when there are pairwise distinct vertices $v_1, \dots, v_m$ of the graph of the instance, with $m \ge K$ and $m \ge 3$, such that $v_j$ is adjacent to $v_{j+1}$ for every $1 \le j < m$ and $v_m$ is adjacent to $v_1$. That is, the graph has a simple cycle with at least $K$ edges and at least three vertices.

results.title: The decision problem LONGEST CYCLE
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: LONGEST CYCLE accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of instances, to an instance of LONGEST CYCLE that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode, and bitstrings that decode to instances that are not well formed, are rejected.

results.title: LONGEST CYCLE is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem LONGEST CYCLE belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to LONGEST CYCLE.

results.title: Binary counter increment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A $k$-bit counter is a vector $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ of bits stored lowest bit first. Incrementing $b$ changes the initial run of $1$ bits $b_0, \dots, b_{t-1}$ to $0$ and then changes the first $0$ bit $b_t$, if there is one, to $1$; if every bit is $1$, all bits become $0$ and no new bit is added. The result is again a $k$-bit counter, and the cost of the increment is the number of bits changed, one unit per…

results.title: Increment adds one with wraparound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored lowest bit first, with bits $b_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and unsigned value $v(b) = \sum_{i < k} b_i 2^i$. If $b'$ is the counter returned by incrementing $b$, then $v(b') = (v(b) + 1) \bmod 2^k$.

results.title: Exact cost of an increment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored lowest bit first, and let $t$ be the length of its initial run of $1$ bits, that is, the largest $t \le k$ with $b_0 = \dots = b_{t-1} = 1$. The cost of incrementing $b$ is $t + 1$ if $t < k$, and $t$ if $t = k$.

results.title: Increment costs at most the width
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits, lowest bit first), the cost of incrementing $b$ is at most $k$.

results.title: Running the binary counter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a width $k$, a $k$-bit counter $b$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the run of $n$ increments from $b$ is defined recursively. The run of $0$ increments returns $b$ at cost zero. The run of $n + 1$ increments performs the run of $n$ increments, then increments the counter it returned and returns the result; its cost is the cost of the $n$-step run plus the cost of that increment.

results.title: Running zero increments
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every width $k$ and every $k$-bit counter $b$, running zero increments from $b$ returns $b$ unchanged at cost zero.

results.title: One more increment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit vector $b$ and every natural number $n$, the bit vector returned by running $n + 1$ increments from $b$ is the increment of the bit vector returned by running $n$ increments from $b$.

results.title: Cost recurrence for the binary counter run
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$ and every $n$, the cost of running $n + 1$ successive increments from $b$ equals the cost of running $n$ increments from $b$ plus the cost of incrementing the counter that the $n$-step run returns.

results.title: Counter value after successive increments
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$ and every $n$, let $v$ be the value of $b$ read as an unsigned binary number with the least significant bit first. After $n$ successive increments starting from $b$, the counter read the same way has value $(v + n) \bmod 2^k$.

results.title: Flip counts of the individual bits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$, $i$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $i < k$, and for each $t$ let $c_t$ be the bit vector returned by running $t$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$. Then the number of $t < n$ such that the bit at position $i$ of $c_t$ (counting from the low-order bit, starting at $0$) differs from the bit at position $i$ of $c_{t+1}$ is $\lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.

results.title: Incrementing the all-ones counter costs the full width
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k$, the cost of incrementing the $k$-bit counter whose $k$ bits are all $1$ is exactly $k$.

results.title: Exact cost of increments from zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs exactly $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.

results.title: Aggregate cost bound for the binary counter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every width $k$ and every $n > 0$, performing $n$ successive increments on the $k$-bit counter that starts with all bits zero costs strictly fewer than $2n$ bit changes in total.

results.title: Lower bound on the cost of increments from zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$ with $k > 0$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs at least $n$.

results.title: Resetting a binary counter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Resetting a bit vector $b$ of width $k$ returns the all-false bit vector of width $k$ and charges cost $1$ for each position of $b$ that holds true, that is, for each bit it changes from true to false.

results.title: Reset returns the all-false counter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned by resetting $b$ are, in order, $k$ copies of false.

results.title: Reset yields the value zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned by resetting $b$, read low-order bit first as an unsigned binary numeral, have value $0$.

results.title: Cost of resetting a binary counter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the cost of resetting $b$ equals the number of positions of $b$ that hold true.

results.title: Reset cost is the Hamming distance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter and $b' = (b'_0, \dots, b'_{k-1})$ the counter returned by resetting $b$. The cost of resetting $b$ equals the number of indices $i < k$ with $b_i \ne b'_i$.

results.title: Reset costs at most the width
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the cost of resetting $b$ is at most $k$.

results.title: Resetting a width-zero counter costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Resetting a bit vector of width $0$ has cost $0$.

results.title: Resetting the all-false counter costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every width $k$, resetting the all-false bit vector of width $k$ has cost $0$.

results.title: Reset is idempotent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by resetting $b$ returns the same counter as resetting $b$ once.

results.title: A second reset costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by resetting $b$ has cost $0$.

results.title: Potential identity for reset
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the cost of resetting $b$ plus the number of $1$ bits in the returned counter equals the number of $1$ bits in $b$.

results.title: Non-request-free frontier exposes a shared output up to congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A non-request-free frontier yields an ACTUAL declared output leaf through canonical par rearrangement. Neither readiness nor a progress result is supplied.

results.title: Exposed shared requests step when declared services are available
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Any actual exposed request fires under the EXISTING all-declared-services availability qualifier, even with ZERO active owned keys or a DONE payload. The Step is constructed from actual offered input syntax, not stored in Available.

results.title: Shared invocation and input worker preserve the combined interface
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A declared shared invocation and ANY typed input worker preserve their EXACT combined linear interface. The actual owned payload is substituted, not the advertised raw protocol; completed receiver annotations remain ambient.

results.title: Inversion of runtime input on a nonshared subject
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nonshared input subject exposes a genuine linear passive or endpoint head. The shared accept alternative is excluded by actual subject nonalias.

results.title: Semantic advance preserves shared-linear separation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Faithful semantic advancement preserves shared/linear separation by its actual owned-domain invariance, including every completed entry.

results.title: Passive head communication preserves runtime typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: At an INITIALLY compatible disjoint interface, a linear passive head retains both actual carrier codes and every runtime continuation guard at unchanged Γ.

results.title: Endpoint head communication preserves runtime typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: At an INITIALLY compatible split, linear endpoint communication transfers ACTUAL v and keeps the receiver's independent advertised payload/tail codes. The Γ-preserving runtime substitution retains all continuation priorities.

results.title: Runtime head communication advances or keeps the interface
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: At an INITIALLY semantically compatible linear interface, actual runtime heads either advance the paired linear subjects faithfully or transfer on a shared service with the EXACT unchanged interface. Mixed shared/linear heads are excluded by source separation, not a finite-fragment erasure or supplied result field.

results.title: Same-name linear guards at a compatible interface communicate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Actual disjoint same-name linear leaves at an INITIALLY compatible interface have opposite directions and construct a canonical Step. Shapes/nonalias are internally exposed outputs in the GLOBAL proof, not caller readiness hypotheses.

results.title: Balanced runtime frontiers are idle or step given availability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A typed balanced runtime frontier with actual persistent service availability is syntactically Idle OR takes an ACTUAL canonical Step. Shared requests are handled even if all owned keys are done; minimum/peer leaves are derived internally.

results.title: Choice selection is the identity on runtime-typed processes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Canonical choice selection is identity on an actually runtime-typed root: there is no sum rule, although replication is admitted. No finiteLinear erasure.

results.title: Subject reduction for runtime typing at compatible interfaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: From a runtime-typed source at an INITIALLY semantically compatible linear interface, ALL5 canonical Step constructors preserve Γ/n, typing and compatibility. The actual residual interface is unchanged OR has one faithful SemanticAdvance. Shared transfers are exact identity; private projection uses the chosen literal pair.

results.title: Subject reduction for runtime typing at balanced interfaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An INITIALLY semantically balanced runtime interface derives compatibility and retains balance and the exact zero-or-one external advance after ANY Step.

results.title: Subject reduction for runtime typing at the empty interface
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An empty linear interface is initially balanced/compatible and remains EXACTLY empty through any runtime Step, including private sessions and shared services.

results.title: Multi-step subject reduction at compatible interfaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: From an INITIALLY compatible runtime interface, finite actual reductions retain typing/compatibility and accumulate a trace of faithful semantic advances. Shared/private identity steps introduce no fake external advancement.

results.title: Multi-step subject reduction at balanced interfaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite reachable state from an INITIALLY balanced runtime interface retains semantic balance and an ACTUAL faithful advancement trace, not progress.

results.title: Multi-step subject reduction at the empty interface
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Finite runtime execution from an empty interface preserves exact empty ownership. This safety result does not identify idle replicas with Cong nil.

results.title: Global runtime progress at balanced interfaces given availability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: GLOBAL progress at arbitrary ambient n/shared Γ/actual balanced Δ/process p, qualified ONLY by runtime typing, INITIAL semantic balance and EXISTING persistent availability of ALL declared signatures. Result is actual Idle syntax OR a canonical Step. No frontier/normal form/readiness/Step/fairness/representative is supplied.

results.title: Closed runtime processes are idle or step given availability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Closed empty-interface runtime progress, at arbitrary passive-name depth, requires the SAME actual all-declared-service availability. Idle includes waiting replicas/accepts and nil; no termination or scheduler fairness is asserted.

results.title: Qualified progress at every reachable runtime state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite canonical reduction from an initially balanced, available typed runtime retains qualified GLOBAL progress. Safety supplies actual balanced residual ownership/advance trace, and Available.reachable supplies current persistent syntax.

results.title: Qualified progress at reachable closed runtime states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Finite reachable empty-interface states retain the same qualified progress; this is one-step safety/progress, not all-schedules eventual responsiveness.

results.title: Metric cost function
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A cost function $d$ assigning to each pair of vertices a value in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid is metric when, for all vertices $x$, $y$, $z$, it is symmetric, $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$, zero on the diagonal, $d(x, x) = 0$, nonnegative, $0 \le d(x, y)$, and satisfies the triangle inequality $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

results.title: Cost of a walk
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in an additive commutative monoid. For a vertex $x$ and a list $L = [y_1, \dots, y_n]$ of vertices, the cost of the walk from $x$ through $L$ is $d(x, y_1) + d(y_1, y_2) + \dots + d(y_{n-1}, y_n)$, and $0$ when $L$ is empty.

results.title: Cost of a closed tour
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a cost function $d$ on the vertices with values in an additive commutative monoid, the cost of the closed tour that visits $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$ in order and returns to its first vertex is $\sum_{i=1}^{k} d(x_{i-1}, x_i) + d(x_k, x_0)$. The empty tour costs $0$.

results.title: Rooted forest in left-child right-sibling form
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A rooted forest with vertices in $\alpha$ is either empty, or consists of a first tree with root $v$, whose subtrees form a forest (the children of $v$), followed by a forest of the remaining trees (the siblings of $v$).

results.title: Preorder of a forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of the vertices of a forest in preorder: empty for the empty forest, and for a forest with first root $v$, children forest $C$ and sibling forest $S$, the vertex $v$, followed by the preorder of $C$, followed by the preorder of $S$.

results.title: Weight of a forest below a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a cost function $d$ and a vertex $p$, the weight of a forest hanging below $p$ is the total cost of its tree edges: each top-level vertex $v$ is joined to $p$ by an edge of cost $d(p, v)$, and each vertex $u$ is joined to each of its children $c$ by an edge of cost $d(u, c)$. The empty forest has weight $0$.

results.title: Path as a forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The forest of a list $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ of vertices is the path $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$: $x_1$ is its only top-level vertex and each $x_{i+1}$ is the only child of $x_i$. The empty list gives the empty forest.

results.title: Preorder walk
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a forest $F$, the preorder walk of $F$ is the preorder walk of $F$ with the empty list as accumulator: a timed computation that returns the vertices of $F$ in preorder, at one time unit per vertex.

results.title: The APPROX-TSP-TOUR algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: CLRS `APPROX-TSP-TOUR`, steps 3 and 4: given a root $r$ and a forest $F$ (the subtrees of a spanning tree with root $r$), return the tour that lists $r$ followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder. results.caption: Theorem

results.title: One step up a parent array
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, assigning to each vertex $v$ either a parent $p(v)$ or no parent. Then $\operatorname{up}(v)$ is the parent $p(v)$ when $v$ has one, and $v$ itself otherwise, so a root stays put.

results.title: Children in a parent array
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing. The children of a vertex $v$ are the vertices $c$ whose parent $p(c)$ is $v$, listed in increasing order.

results.title: Forest of a parent array below a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a vertex $v$, the forest below $v$ of depth $k$ is empty when $k = 0$. For depth $k + 1$ it has one tree for each child $c$ of $v$ (each vertex whose parent is $v$), in increasing order of $c$, namely $c$ with the forest below $c$ of depth $k$ as its subtrees.

results.title: Parent tree
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, and let a step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex without parent in place. The parent array $p$ is a parent tree with root $r$ when $r$ has no parent and every vertex reaches $r$ after finitely many steps up.

For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, a vertex $u$ lies strictly below a vertex $v$, at most $k$ levels down, when for some $j < k$ the vertex reached from $u$ after $j$ steps up has parent $v$.

results.title: Every non-root vertex lies below the root
results.caption: Theorem

Then every vertex $u \ne r$ lies strictly below $r$, at most $n$ levels down: for some $j < n$, the vertex reached from $u$ after $j$ steps up has parent $r$.

results.title: The forest of a parent tree spans all vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, forming a parent tree with root $r$. Then $r$ together with the forest below $r$ of depth $n$ built from $p$ is a spanning tree of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest in preorder lists every vertex exactly once.

results.title: Symmetrized edge weights
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Neighbours in the complete adjacency
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all vertices $u, v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $v$ is listed among the neighbours of $u$ in the complete graph as an ordered adjacency if and only if $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the complete simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, $u \ne v$.

results.title: Prim's tree
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, Prim's tree is the simple graph on these vertices in which distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when one of them is the parent of the other in Prim's parent array for $d$ and $r$.

results.title: Prim's tree is a spanning tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in any linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and any root $r$, Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a tree on all of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, a spanning tree of the complete graph.

results.title: Prim's tree is a minimum spanning tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d(u,v)$ be real costs on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $r$ be a vertex, and weigh each edge $\{u, v\}$ by $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$. Then Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a tree, and for every tree $H$ on these vertices the total weight of the edges of Prim's tree is at most the total weight of the edges of $H$.

results.title: Prim's forest spans all vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero and a commutative addition, let $d$ assign a weight in $W$ to each ordered pair of vertices of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $r$ be a vertex. Then $r$ together with Prim's forest for $d$ and $r$ is a spanning tree of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest in preorder lists every vertex exactly once.

results.title: The tour from Prim's tree is a tour
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and any root $r$, the list returned by APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a permutation of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$: it visits every vertex exactly once.

results.title: APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree is a 2-approximation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ be a real metric cost on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfying the triangle inequality), and let $r$ be a vertex. Then the cost of the closed tour through the list returned by APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is at most twice the cost of the closed tour through $H$, for every list $H$ that visits each of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ exactly once.

results.title: Edges of the complete graph $K_n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the complete board is the finite set of edges of the complete graph $K_n$ on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, that is, the set of all unordered pairs $\{i, j\}$ of distinct vertices $i \ne j$.

results.title: Free elements of a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For finite sets $X$ (the board), $M$ (the elements claimed by Maker) and $R$ (the elements claimed by Breaker), the free elements are the elements of $X$ claimed by neither player, that is, the set $X \setminus (M \cup R)$.

results.title: Maker wins the biased game with Breaker moving first
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite board $X$, a bias $b \in \mathbb{N}$ and a target property of Maker's claimed set, Maker wins the $(1 : b)$ Maker-Breaker game on $X$ in which Breaker moves first when, for every set $F \subseteq X$ of exactly $\min(b, |X|)$ elements that Breaker may claim in his first move, Maker can force a win when it is his turn at the position where he has claimed nothing and Breaker has claimed $F$.

results.title: Maker's Hamiltonicity target
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, a set $C$ of unordered pairs of vertices from $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ meets the Hamiltonicity target when the simple graph on these $n$ vertices whose edges are the pairs of distinct vertices in $C$ is Hamiltonian: it has a cycle passing through every vertex exactly once, with the convention that the one-vertex graph is Hamiltonian.
